title: A creatinine of 3.1 and a dribble
presentation: A 74-year-old man presents with three days of nausea, poor appetite and difficulty passing urine: frequency, a weak stream, waking four times a night, and since this morning only a dribble. Triage labs: creatinine 3.1 mg/dL (1.0 six months ago), BUN 58, K 5.6, HCO3 19, Na 137. HR 92, BP 148/88, T 36.9 C.

stages.label: History
stages.text: Past history: hypertension, osteoarthritis of both knees, and prostatic symptoms for two years that he has never had treated. Medications: lisinopril 20 mg daily and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily for years. Three weeks ago he started over-the-counter naproxen 500 mg twice daily for his knees. One week ago he started diphenhydramine 50 mg at night for sleep. He has deliberately cut down on fluids 'so I don't have to keep going'. No haematuria, no flank pain, no fever, no rash, no joint swelling, no recent contrast, antibiotics or new prescriptions. No vomiting or diarrhoea. No known kidney disease.
stages.prompt: Organise your differential into prerenal, intrinsic and post-renal causes. Before any laboratory test, what one bedside thing do you want?
stages.learner_goal: Use the three-bucket framework, flag the NSAID/ACE inhibitor/diuretic combination and the new anticholinergic, and ask for a bladder scan or catheter before anything else.

stages.label: Exam
stages.text: HR 92, BP 148/88 lying and 140/84 standing. Mucous membranes slightly dry, JVP low-normal, no oedema. Abdomen: a tense, dull, mildly tender suprapubic mass rising to the umbilicus. Rectal examination: smoothly enlarged prostate, no nodules, normal anal tone. No rash, no joint effusions. Lungs clear.
stages.prompt: Which test first, and what does it tell you? Commit to the main mechanism of his kidney injury and say what else is contributing.
stages.learner_goal: Recognise retention on exam, confirm it with a bladder scan, and use the urinalysis and drug history to weigh obstruction against prerenal and intrinsic causes.

available_tests.urinalysis: Specific gravity 1.012, pH 6, no blood, trace protein, no leukocytes or nitrites. Microscopy: occasional hyaline casts, no granular or muddy brown casts, no red cell casts, no white cells, no crystals.
available_tests.urine electrolytes: Urine sodium 48 mEq/L, urine creatinine 42 mg/dL; FENa 2.4% (on a thiazide). Urine urea 180 mg/dL; FEUrea 41%.
available_tests.renal ultrasound: Bilateral moderate hydronephrosis with dilated ureters to the bladder. Bladder distended with a thickened wall. Kidneys 11.2 and 11.5 cm with preserved cortical thickness. No stones.
available_tests.cbc: Hb 13.4 g/dL, WBC 8.9 x10^9/L with a normal eosinophil count, platelets 230.
available_tests.ecg: Sinus rhythm 90, no peaked T waves, QRS 92 ms.
available_tests.psa: Deferred: PSA is unreliable during retention and after catheterisation.

stages.label: After the catheter
stages.text: A urethral catheter passes easily and drains 1,400 mL of clear urine immediately. Ultrasound shows bilateral moderate hydronephrosis with a thick-walled bladder and normal-sized kidneys. Urinalysis is bland with hyaline casts only. Naproxen, lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide and diphenhydramine are held. Over the next 12 hours he passes 4.2 L of urine. At 24 hours creatinine is 2.2 and K 4.6; at 72 hours creatinine is 1.3.
stages.prompt: What happened here, and what contributed? How do you manage the next 48 hours, and what goes on his discharge medication list?
stages.learner_goal: Name obstructive AKI with haemodynamic contributors, manage post-obstructive diuresis and hyperkalaemia, and plan drug review, an alpha-blocker and urology follow-up.

diagnosis: Acute kidney injury from acute urinary retention (bilateral obstructive uropathy due to benign prostatic hyperplasia precipitated by an anticholinergic), with a prerenal contribution from NSAID, ACE inhibitor and thiazide
key_clues: New lower urinary tract symptoms progressing to a dribble in a man with untreated prostatic symptoms
Diphenhydramine started one week ago (anticholinergic precipitant of retention)
Palpable, dull suprapubic mass with a post-void residual of 1,150 mL and bilateral hydronephrosis
Naproxen plus lisinopril plus hydrochlorothiazide with reduced fluid intake
Bland urine sediment with no granular casts
Creatinine falls to 1.3 within 72 hours of catheter drainage

distractors.name: Prerenal AKI from poor intake and the NSAID/ACE inhibitor/diuretic combination
distractors.why_not: Contributes, but there is no orthostasis, a 1.4 L bladder and bilateral hydronephrosis explain the injury, and creatinine fell only after the catheter.

distractors.name: Acute tubular necrosis
distractors.why_not: Urine sediment is bland with no granular casts, and creatinine fell to 1.3 within 72 hours of decompression; ATN recovers over one to three weeks.

distractors.name: Acute interstitial nephritis from naproxen
distractors.why_not: No pyuria, white cell casts, rash, fever or eosinophilia, and recovery was too fast.

distractors.name: Prostate cancer with obstruction
distractors.why_not: Prostate is smooth without nodules; PSA cannot be interpreted during retention, so check it after recovery.

distractors.name: Rhabdomyolysis
distractors.why_not: CK is normal and the dipstick is negative for blood.

distractors.name: Bilateral renal artery stenosis unmasked by the ACE inhibitor
distractors.why_not: Kidneys are symmetric and normal sized, and hydronephrosis provides the explanation.

rubric.description: Frames the differential as prerenal, intrinsic and post-renal
rubric.concept: AKI is sorted into prerenal, intrinsic and post-renal before anything else

rubric.description: Raises obstruction or retention from the history alone
rubric.concept: New lower urinary tract symptoms with AKI means obstruction until the bladder is scanned

rubric.description: Flags the NSAID, ACE inhibitor and thiazide combination and the new anticholinergic
rubric.concept: The triple whammy (NSAID + RAAS blocker + diuretic) and anticholinergics in BPH are the commonest avoidable causes of AKI in older men

rubric.description: Asks for a bladder scan or catheter (or renal ultrasound) before or alongside the labs
rubric.concept: Bladder scan is the first test in AKI: obstruction is the most quickly reversible cause

rubric.description: Looks at the urine (dipstick, sediment, urine sodium or FEUrea) and knows FENa is unreliable on a diuretic
rubric.concept: Urine sediment separates ATN and interstitial nephritis from prerenal and obstructive AKI; FEUrea replaces FENa on diuretics

rubric.description: Final diagnosis names obstruction or urinary retention as the main mechanism
rubric.concept: Obstructive AKI from acute urinary retention

rubric.description: Decompresses the bladder with a catheter and leaves it in
rubric.concept: Relief of obstruction is the treatment; the earlier the relief, the more complete the recovery

rubric.description: Stops the NSAID and anticholinergic, and holds the ACE inhibitor and diuretic until recovery
rubric.concept: Remove haemodynamic insults during AKI; restart RAAS blockade only after recovery

rubric.description: Anticipates post-obstructive diuresis: monitors urine output and electrolytes and replaces losses when needed
rubric.concept: Post-obstructive diuresis can cause volume depletion and electrolyte loss in the first 24 to 48 hours

management_summary: Leave the catheter in. Expect post-obstructive diuresis: hourly urine output, daily weights, and electrolytes (potassium, sodium, magnesium, phosphate) every 6 to 12 hours for the first 24 hours; replace roughly half of the urine output with 0.45% saline only if he becomes volume deplete or the output exceeds about 200 mL/h for several hours, because most of the diuresis is physiological off-loading. Repeat ECG and potassium, and treat hyperkalaemia if it rises or the ECG changes. Stop naproxen and diphenhydramine permanently; hold lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide until creatinine is back to baseline, then restart one at a time with a creatinine check at one week. Start tamsulosin, plan a trial of void in one to two weeks with urology follow-up, and check PSA after the acute episode. Paracetamol and topical NSAID for the knees.
teaching_points: Every AKI gets three questions in order: is the bladder full (bladder scan or catheter), is the patient volume deplete, and what is in the urine. Obstruction is the most quickly reversible cause and the easiest to miss in a man with 'just prostate symptoms'.

NSAID plus ACE inhibitor or ARB plus diuretic, the 'triple whammy', removes the kidney's defences against hypoperfusion: prostaglandin-dependent afferent dilatation, angiotensin-dependent efferent constriction, and volume. Add a new anticholinergic in a man with BPH and retention follows.

Urine indices have caveats: FENa is uninterpretable on a diuretic (use FEUrea; under 35% suggests prerenal), and obstruction can give any pattern. A bland sediment argues against ATN and interstitial nephritis; the speed of recovery after relief is the final arbiter.
After decompression, monitor for post-obstructive diuresis and electrolyte loss, and restart renin-angiotensin blockade only once the kidney has recovered.
